items.summary:
‘Elbow noodles’ for a pet? Obsessed with labels, and jam-packed with condiments, it could only be author and chef Carla Lalli …

Cheese
I pretty much always have parm or grana padano, and pecorino, for pasta, Caesar salad or a dressing. I’ll have a parmesan rind in the mix, too, for when I’m cooking beans or grains. Then, there’s snacking cheese: sliced cheddar, Pepper Jack or muenster from the deli section for a quesadilla when Cosmo [Lalli’s son] gets home. I love mozzarella sticks for a protein snack, or sometimes when I’m alone, I’ll melt them on stir-fried rice with kimchi, or Korean rice cakes. I always have them in the summer when I go to the beach, too.

Marge’s food
This is my dog’s food. The usual recipe is a mix of ground minced turkey, minced beef, chicken liver, chicken gizzards, carrot, butternut squash, some frozen kale or spinach, elbow noodles and rice. I truly did not think I would ever be this person, but she’s so picky about her food … I wonder why! But I did get sick of buying food and her leaving half of it behind.

As a Brit, there are plenty of reasons for me not to embrace Thanksgiving, most of all because it isn’t actually a British holiday, and least of all because we already have quite enough occasions to eat ourselves silly between now and January. And yet, every November, as the days grow shorter and darker and colder, I find myself rather taken with the idea of hosting a seasonal dinner for friends. If Christmas is more formal and family-focused, then Thanksgiving feels like a prime opportunity to get pals around the table, eat until you need to undo your top trouser button, and take a moment to appreciate what you have. And if that means borrowing a few ideas from across the Atlantic – a warming spiced pumpkin pie, say, or a dish of fruity stuffing and a sharp cranberry sauce – well, there’s no reason we can’t make them our own.

items.title: Rachel Roddy’s recipe for pasta all’arrabbiata with red onion and plums | A kitchen in Rome
items.summary:
Much like tomato, the plum has a natural acidity and sweetness that works brilliantly in a delightfully jammy pasta sauce

Standing on platform 2 at Baker Street station a few weeks ago, a grey creature scuttled under the raised tracks. “You’re never more than six feet away from a rat in London,” I said to my Roman son. “It’s a mouse, Mum,” was his hardboiled reply to my rehashing of an urban myth. A myth that turns out to be inaccurate, according to Dr David Cowan, whose research on the subject resulted in estimates of anything from 10ft-164ft: in other words, while it’s impossible to know for sure, in certain areas you might be very close to a rat.

The same can be said about wild plum trees all over the world. While it’s impossible to know exactly, even in dense urban areas, you might be very close to a wild plum tree or, more correctly, a cultivated plum that has gone feral. Hedgerows, field margins, woodland edges, abandoned parks and wastelands are all places in which you might find yourself close to a plum tree; its branches decorated with fruit, some the size of marbles, others lozenges or eggs, and their spectrum of colour ranging from deep purple to powdery light blue, red, pink, gold and green.

What a night. On Sunday, November 15, the winners of the 2026 Eater Awards, presented by Capital One, celebrated together at Nine Orchard in NYC. More than 200 chefs, restaurateurs, bartenders, and friends of Eater — many of whom traveled across the country to be there — partook in live portraiture, custom engraving, and, of course, plenty of food and drink.

Now in its 17th year, the Eater Awards recognize the year’s best new restaurants, bakeries, bars, dishes, and chefs in markets across the U.S.. More than 30 Eater staffers and contributors spent months traveling to 44 cities to weigh contenders on food, service, atmosphere, and the stories behind them. The prize? A tomato can trophy. And yes, they’re real.

The night started off strong with photos at the tomato can-wrapped step-and-repeat and a welcome shot of Zbiotics, before guests headed up to the roof of Nine Orchard for panoramic views and more fun. The party was filled with unique moments, from custom lighter engraving presented by Toast to live water color portraits presented by Capital One. Rounds of dishes inspired by the winning restaurants were passed. 

A champagne toast commemorated the resiliency of the hospitality industry. “Thank you for what you do, every single day, to bolster your team, your community, and the restaurant industry at large,” said Eater editor in chief Stephanie Wu.

items.title: The 38 Best London Restaurants, According to Eater’s Local Dining Expert
items.summary:
The story of the London food scene is one that includes dim sum, Sunday roasts, curries, pizza, sinasir, rarebits, banh mi, udon, pepper pot, sweetbread suya, and natural wine. Across cuisines, neighborhoods, and price points, all these dishes and drinks place London among the very best and most diverse places to eat in the world.

This guide, which I’ve been compiling and iterating on for the better part of the last decade, aims to reflect the best food and most important restaurants in the capital. I want this map to help you navigate a city in which it is all too easy to eat poorly, but in which it is increasingly inexcusable to do so. It will showcase a mix of over three dozen restaurants, which have all done outstanding things in extraordinary times: emerging, surviving, thriving, and continuing to enrich the city and its food culture through more than half a decade of unprecedented change and tumult.

We update this list regularly to make sure it reflects the ever-changing London dining scene. Our write-ups include insider tips, as well as a rough range of pricing for each destination — ranging from $ for quick, inexpensive meals with dishes largely under $10 (or the equivalent in pounds), to $$$$ for places where entrees exceed $30.

items.title: Help! Why does my apple pie always have a soggy base? | Kitchen aide
items.summary:
Direct the heat and minimise the moisture to save your pastry from a saturated bottom, says our panel of pie pros

Why does the pastry base of my apple pie always come out soggy? What am I doing wrong?
Sophie, by email
“The very first thing I would say is that Sophie has got to look at her filling, and how wet it is,” says Calum Franklin, author of The Modern Pie Maker and all-round pie Yoda. “Apples contain quite a lot of water already, so you don’t generally need to add any extra liquid to the filling.” Instead, he’d simply cook the apples with sugar: “Just let them break down.”

That said, Sophie could always consider including some sort of barrier, too, says Dee Rettali, co-founder of Fortitude Bakehouse in London: “My mother was an amazing baker, and she always sprinkled a very fine crumble mix [just sugar and flour, no fat] on the bottom of her pie before putting in any fruit. That will then absorb most of the liquid.”

However, these ricotta-and-parmesan-based dumplings are so easy to throw together, and always come out light and with just the right amount of squidge. Sage and brown butter feels the right sauce at this time of year, but you could serve them with a simple tomato sauce instead. Any leftover dumplings work a treat thrown into a brothy, minestrone-type soup.

items.title: Squash and chickpea curry, and whipped beans with radicchio: Marie Mitchell’s sweet-and-sour recipes
items.summary:
Pucker up for squash and tamarind curry with stewed chickpeas and coriander, or how about whipped cannellini beans with leeks, roast radicchio and parmesan?

Who doesn’t love sweet and sour? If you’re complaining that you don’t right now, then you’re lying – it’s an almost perfect pairing. Here, I’m playing with the sweet-and-sour notes of vinegar and the tang of tamarind in two dishes that are on repeat in our house. Dinners for when you want to spend more time on the sofa and less time in the kitchen.
